“Autumn Crocus” vase by Émile Gallé

A tall Nancy glass vase that grows like its subject: a pink-streaked stem swells up from a dark bulb-shaped foot and carries applied orange and violet crocus flowers.

Context

The Met records the object as a vase with tray, glass, ca. 1900, 44.1 × 11.7 × 11.7 cm, designed by Émile Gallé (1846–1904) and made by Établissements Gallé; gift of Lloyd and Barbara Macklowe, 1984. The Met marks it public domain. The Met 1984.553.

Wikipedia describes Gallé as a trained botanist, a major innovator of French Art Nouveau, and founder and first president (1901) of the École de Nancy; the 1900 Paris Exposition was the summit of his fame. Wikipedia: Émile Gallé.

Observed

  • The vase is tall and narrow. It widens slowly from a thin neck-like lower stem to a rounded top, then closes slightly at the lip.
  • Fine pink threads run vertically up the frosted, pale body; toward the base they deepen into magenta streaks.
  • One orange crocus with yellow stamens and two violet-blue crocuses stand near the top, raised from the surface. A long violet leaf and a thin orange stem run down the body.
  • The foot is a dark, lobed, bulb-like mass in aubergine with orange inclusions.
  • The photograph shows the vase against a plain white ground.

Why it belongs

The form follows the plant: bulb at the foot, a long stem, and flowers at the top. This is the Nancy School version of the style’s idea that structure and ornament grow from one natural form.

The colours here are more vivid than the grammar’s earthy palette, but they come from the flower itself and sit on a pale, soft ground.

Borrow

Let a tall container or column narrow and swell like a stem, with its weight at the base.

Use fine vertical threads of one tint as a texture that deepens toward one end.
